passage:
Subject: Ritwik's fall at lunch
Hi Gurpreet,
Quick note before his parents call. When I reached the swings, Ritwik was sitting in the sand holding his wrist. I knelt and asked only, "What happened?" He said, "I was swinging high and my hand slipped. Then I fell." I wrote that in my diary at 12:40, word for word.
By 2 pm, after his friends had crowded round, he was saying someone pushed him. I didn't argue. I asked, "What do you remember now?" and wrote that down too, with the time.
Can we agree that on duty we ask "What happened?" first, and never "Did someone push you?" Each time a child tells it, the story gets built again, and our questions shape the building.
Thanks,
Madhuri

qa.q: At what time did Madhuri write down Ritwik's first account?
qa.a: At 12:40, word for word.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri decide not to argue when Ritwik later said someone pushed him?
qa.a: Madhuri wanted to understand Ritwik's memory without steering it either way, so Madhuri simply asked what he remembered now and recorded that too.

qa.q: What does Madhuri ask Gurpreet to agree to, and why is that a better choice on duty?
qa.a: To ask "What happened?" first instead of "Did someone push you?", so the adult's question doesn't plant a push that never happened.

qa.q: How might Ritwik's parents be helped by Madhuri's two timed notes?
qa.a: They can see what Ritwik said right after the fall and how the story changed after his friends crowded round, instead of hearing only one confident version.

passage: "Santosh the detective," you called me, Hansa. Fine, I'll explain the phone notes. Last Sunday my daughter Chinki ran in from the courtyard crying, knee scraped. My first thought was, did those Sharma boys push her? But I stopped myself. I just held her and asked, "What happened, Chinki?" She hiccupped. "I ran after the kitten and the step was there." That's all. I typed it into my phone right then, with the time. Evening comes, my mother asks her, "Did those boys push you?" and Chinki nods, big eyes. "Yes, they pushed." If I hadn't written down the first version, I'd have gone next door to fight. Instead I showed Amma my note. She laughed and said, "Arre, I put the boys in her head."

passage: I'm Karthik, and I share a staffroom with Asif, who has taught Class 3 for two years. On Friday a window in his room cracked during break, with three children near it. The principal came in asking, "Was it the cricket ball?" Asif gently took over. He sat each child down on their own and said, "Tell me everything from when the bell rang." No names, no ball, no stick. He wrote their words in a notebook straight away, before they had lunch together. One girl said a pigeon flew into the glass. A boy said a door slammed. Honestly, I thought he was wasting time. But by Monday all three children were talking about a ball, and Asif's Friday notes were the only clean record. Later he told me, "Every time they retell it, they're building it again."

qa.q: What did Asif say to each child?
qa.a: "Tell me everything from when the bell rang."

qa.q: Why did Asif want the children's words written down before lunch?
qa.a: Asif expected their stories to blend once they talked together, so he wanted each child's own account while it was fresh.

qa.q: The principal suggested a cricket ball. What made Asif's approach better at that point?
qa.a: Asif suggested no cause and spoke to each child alone, so the Friday notes caught what each remembered before the ball entered their stories.

qa.q: How did Karthik's view of Asif's method change?
qa.a: Karthik first thought Asif was wasting time, but on Monday saw that the Friday notes were the only clean record.

Tuesday. Joseph, the senior teacher, was in the corridor with his register when little Mitu came in from recess holding a crushed paper boat, lip trembling. Anjali, twenty-four and in her first year, crouched down. She didn't ask who did it. She asked, "What happened?" Mitu said, "I put it on the step and I sat on it by mistake." Anjali wrote it in her notebook with the time, 11:05.
Wednesday. Mitu's mother came to the gate, upset. "She says Rahul crushed it." At home, Joseph learned, the first question had been, "Did someone break it?"
Friday. At the short parents' meeting, Anjali read her note aloud, word for word. Mitu's mother went quiet, then nodded. Joseph noticed how Anjali never said the child was lying, only that stories change as they are asked about.

qa.q: What time did Anjali write in her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote 11:05.

qa.q: What does Anjali's refusal to call Mitu a liar suggest about her understanding of memory?
qa.a: It suggests Anjali stays calm and caring, understanding that memory reshapes itself with each question rather than thinking the child is dishonest.

qa.q: Which choice by Anjali made the difference on Friday, and why?
qa.a: Asking an open "What happened?" and writing the answer down with the time gave an early, unshaped account to compare later.

qa.q: How might Mitu's mother see the situation after hearing the note?
qa.a: She might realise her own question, "Did someone break it?", may have planted Rahul, and feel relieved no child was being unfair to Mitu.

grounding: A colleague observes a teacher ask an open question and record the child's account early, before later questions reshape it.

passage:
Devika, you're new to teaching, so let an old headmaster tell you one thing. In my second year as a young teacher in Malegaon, when the children called me Wasim Sir and I was twenty-four and nervous, two boys brought me a library book torn right down the spine. Each said the other did it. My first thought was to ask, "Did you pull it, Salim?" I stopped. Instead I took them separately and asked each one, "Tell me what happened, from the start." I wrote down every word before lunch.
By the next morning, both fathers were in my office, with new stories: a push, a threat, a third boy. But I had my notes. In the first version, both boys had been pulling the book at once to see a picture of a whale. No villain. Just a whale. Memory is built again each time someone asks, beta. Ask plainly, and write it early.

qa.q: What were the two boys trying to see in the book?
qa.a: They were both pulling at once to see a picture of a whale.

qa.q: Why did Wasim Sir stop himself from asking "Did you pull it, Salim?"
qa.a: Though young and nervous, he understood that a pointed question could shape the boy's account, so he chose to ask plainly instead.

qa.q: What could Devika do the next time children give competing stories?
qa.a: Talk to each child separately, ask "What happened?" without suggesting names or details, and write their words down that same day.

qa.q: How might the two fathers feel when shown the first written account?
qa.a: They might feel embarrassed or relieved that neither boy was a villain, and see how their own questions had grown the story.

grounding: An elder recalls asking open questions and recording children's accounts early, before later questions reshaped them.
